chapter_theme: A single song at Thiruvirkudi (திருவிற்குடி): women who measure every mind and stand in the golden street like a rutting elephant, and the poet who fears fading in their net like an elephant in a pit; the praise is a battle in drum syllables and Brahma imprisoned.

814.reading: The poet describes women with breasts lovelier than in a painting, waists thin as a hair, who measure every mind as one would count the sea's sand, with musky hair, fish-like eyes and bright laughter, speaking spells of infatuation and standing in the golden street like a green-gem peacock or a rutting elephant, and asks whether, caught in their net, he will fade like an elephant that has fallen into a pit. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, conch and drums sounding, the sea, the mountains of the directions and the serpent's hoods shaken as the wicked Suras die; Murugan gave Indra back his place and married the parrot-like Devayanai, and seized Brahma, beat his head and imprisoned him to his shame; he is lord at Virkudi praised by the freed.
814.nuance: சித்தம் அத்தனையும் முற்று அளப்ப கடல் மொய்த்த சிற்றுமணலுக்கும் எட்டியது: the women can measure a whole mind as if counting the sea's grains, so their skill is knowledge of men. The poet becomes the elephant trapped in a pit (குழி உற்ற அத்தி), after the women were compared to a rutting elephant (அத்தி ஒத்த மதம்). Brahma's imprisonment is given without its usual cause.

links.note: 814 asks whether, caught in the courtesans' net, he will fade like an elephant fallen into a pit (வலைபட்டு உழைத்து குழி உற்ற அத்தியென மங்குவேனா). Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). Both picture the man not as seduced but as sunk in a hole he cannot climb out of.
